parts.label: (i)
parts.official_mark_scheme_text: Substitute in $uv$, expand and use $i^2=-1$ — M1. Obtain $uv=-11-5\sqrt3i$ — A1. EITHER substitute in $u/v$ and multiply numerator and denominator by the conjugate of $v$, or equivalent — M1; obtain numerator $-7+7\sqrt3i$ or denominator 7 — A1; obtain $-1+\sqrt3i$ — A1. OR substitute in $u/v$, equate to $x+iy$ and solve for $x$ or $y$ — M1; guidance equations $-3\sqrt3=\sqrt3x-2y$, $1=2x+\sqrt3y$; obtain $x=-1$ or $y=\sqrt3$ — A1; obtain $-1+\sqrt3i$ — A1. Total: 5.

parts.label: (ii)
parts.official_mark_scheme_text: Show the points $A$ and $B$ representing $u$ and $v$ in relatively correct positions — B1. Carry out a complete method for finding $\angle AOB$, e.g. calculate $\arg(u/v)$ — M1. If using $\theta=\tan^{-1}(-\sqrt3)$, refer to $\arg(u/v)$. Official alternatives include: use separate arguments with $\tan a=-\frac1{3\sqrt3}$ and $\tan b=\frac2{\sqrt3}$, so $\tan(a-b)=\frac{-1/(3\sqrt3)-2/\sqrt3}{1-2/9}=-\sqrt3$; use a scalar product, $\cos\theta=\frac{(-3\sqrt3)(\sqrt3)+(1)(2)}{\sqrt7\sqrt{28}}=\frac{-9+2}{14}=-\frac12$; or use the cosine rule, $\cos\theta=\frac{28+7-49}{2\sqrt{28}\sqrt7}=-\frac12$. Prove $\angle AOB=\frac{2\pi}{3}$ — A1. Guidance: given answer, check working carefully. Total: 3.
